query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys, toughness retention under demanding conditions is governed by the interplay between irradiation/thermal‐driven defect recombination (which preserves a homogeneous, ductile microstructure) and a critical degree of grain boundary elemental segregation that leads to nanoscale brittle precipitate formation, thereby degrading toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, fine-grained (nanocrystalline/ultrafine) refractory HEA (e.g., W-Ta-Cr-V composition) with a homogeneous distribution of elements and no pre-existing precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled irradiation at high temperature (e.g., ~1073 K up to ~8 dpa) while performing a parallel test with a minor alloying addition (e.g., Hf) that is expected to mitigate grain boundary segregation.
generation.conditions: Thin film samples processed via magnetron sputtering; irradiation performed under constant temperature (around 1073 K) with incremental increases in dose; mechanical characterization (e.g., nanoindentation and toughness/fracture measurements) before and after irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry and the formation (or absence) of nanoscale precipitates (e.g., Cr-V rich clusters) that can embrittle the HEA.
generation.mechanism: Under irradiation or elevated temperatures, the severe lattice distortion in HEAs promotes similar mobilities of vacancies and interstitials, enhancing defect recombination and preserving toughness. However, beyond a critical irradiation dose (or thermal exposure), elevated defect mobility can also drive localized elemental segregation at grain boundaries, leading to the nucleation and growth of brittle precipitates that reduce resistance to crack propagation. A minor addition of an element like Hf is hypothesized to stabilize the grain boundary composition and counteract segregation, thereby retaining toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The baseline alloy will maintain high toughness up to a threshold irradiation dose, beyond which measurable formation of nanoscale grain boundary precipitates occurs accompanied by a reduction in toughness. In contrast, the Hf-modified alloy will exhibit delayed or reduced precipitate formation and retain higher toughness under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited HEA state with a homogeneous element distribution, exhibiting high defect recombination rates and no significant precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanocrystalline/ultrafine-grained refractory HEAs subjected to temperatures between room temperature and ~1073 K and irradiation doses in the range of 0 to roughly 8–10 dpa, where defect kinetics and segregation effects are active.
generation.uncertainty: The exact irradiation dose threshold at which deleterious grain boundary segregation and precipitate formation occur, as well as the quantitative effect of minor Hf addition on suppressing segregation, remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with the baseline composition (e.g., W-Ta-Cr-V) and one with a minor addition of Hf. Subject both to stepwise irradiation at ~1073 K, increasing the dpa gradually (up to ~8–10 dpa). Characterize microstructure (through TEM and APT) for precipitate nucleation at grain boundaries and perform mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness or nanoindentation-based assessments) before and after irradiation.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and precipitate density/size (using APT and TEM)
Mechanical toughness metrics (e.g., fracture toughness, ductility) before and after irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (a) both the baseline and Hf-modified alloys show similar levels of grain boundary precipitate formation and deterioration in toughness at matching irradiation doses, or (b) if the addition of Hf does not significantly delay or reduce the onset of segregation-induced embrittlement relative to the baseline, contrary to the predicted behavior.
